title: Choose the visual world
question: The roll assigned The Stratigraphic Log. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: The Stratigraphic Log
options.lineage: geologists' graphic logs and stratigraphic columns, FGDC lithology patterns
options.thesis: The page is one geologist's column, logged from the summit of Everest down to the inner core.
materials: flat lithology fills with standard rock patterns
log-sheet title block and depth axis
options.viewport: A log-sheet title block, a depth axis reading +8,849 m, and the column opening on Everest's marine limestone, its top edge the summit profile.
options.risk: Reads as a printed handout if the column stops being the page and turns into a picture beside the text.

raised.raise: Each layer's height is its real depth range at a stated scale; scale changes are drawn as explicit break marks.
Sourced boundaries draw solid; anything illustrative or interpolated draws dashed and is labelled.
Depth and temperature print into the log's own margin columns as you pass, not in a floating HUD.
In the mantle, the pointer's wake stirs a visible convection field drawn in the column's pattern ink.
The column's fixed track grid is the only geometry; nothing floats off it.

options.label: The Core Tray
options.lineage: drill-core boxes in a geology lab
options.thesis: The descent laid out as one continuous core sample, boxed in trays with stencilled depth blocks.
options.viewport: The first tray row: a cylinder of summit limestone with fossils, a depth block reading 8,849 m.
options.risk: The most literal geology artifact on the list, and a real core can't come from below ~12 km, so the conceit is visibly fictional past the crust.

options.label: One Layer per Screen
options.thesis: Every stop on the way down fills the screen, one flick from the next.
options.viewport: Everest's summit full-bleed, depth as the 'author line' low left, a rail of glyphs: inspect, drag plates, °C, sources.
options.case: Students know this form by heart and it fits a 2–5 minute visit; loses on clarity because hard snaps break the continuous descent.
options.risk: Snap paging hides how far apart the layers really are, and it can read as a social-media parody.

options.label: Labanotation Score
options.thesis: A center staff where each block's length is an exact measure.
options.viewport: A vertical staff with layer blocks sized to depth.
options.case: Fuses poorly: geology students don't read dance notation.
options.kept: Length is exact: layer heights follow real depth at a stated scale.

options.label: Sewing Pattern Tissue
options.thesis: Layers as tissue pieces, plates pinned until their notches meet.
options.viewport: A folded tissue map of Earth's layers.
options.case: Fuses poorly: nothing about the Earth's interior lives in a sewing room.
options.kept: Committed vs. uncommitted: solid lines for sourced facts, dashed for illustrative.

options.label: Phosphor Terminal
options.thesis: The descent as a scrolling transcript.
options.case: Fuses poorly: a transcript can't show layers or scale.
options.kept: State prints itself: readouts are log entries, not chrome.

options.label: Bioluminescent Wake
options.viewport: A dark field lit by the cursor's wake.
options.case: Fuses poorly: an ocean world misreads rock, though its current field suits convection.
options.kept: The pointer's wake makes mantle convection visible.

options.label: ANSI Bulletin Board
options.viewport: Block-art Everest over a numbered menu.
options.case: Fuses poorly: no geology student meets the Earth through a BBS.
options.kept: One fixed grid is the only geometry.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: The classic 'journey to the center' scroll story, executed impeccably.
canonCard.viewport: A night-sky Everest silhouette, a big title, and a depth meter pinned to the side.
canonCard.risk: Looks like every Earth-layers explainer on the web.
